issues: The big bang is better described as a rapid expansion of space itself, not an "explosion from a single point". Recorded as printed.

The box gives average crust thickness as 8–40 km but continental crust as 30–50 km; continental crust is commonly 30–70 km thick. "Oceanic crust age: 200 million years" means its maximum age (most is younger). Recorded as printed.
The text calls the lithosphere the "upper part of mantle"; the lithosphere is the crust plus the uppermost mantle, and the asthenosphere lies below it within the upper mantle. Recorded as printed.

The Conrad discontinuity is actually a boundary inside the continental crust (between upper and lower crust), not between the hydrosphere and the crust. The mantle–core boundary was identified by Beno Gutenberg (working with Emil Wiechert) in 1913–1914; the book's "Weichert Guttenberg in 1912" merges two names. The spelling of "Gutenberg" also varies on the page (Guttenburg, Guttenbuerg, Guttenberg). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Globe map captioned "Pangaea": the single supercontinent with North America, South America, Africa, Eurasia, India, Antarctica and Australia joined together.

World map captioned "Seven Major Tectonic Plates" (title "MAJOR TECTONIC PLATES"), with plate boundaries and movement arrows: Eurasian, North American, Pacific, Juan de Fuca, Caribbean, Cocos, Nazca, South American, African, Arabian, Indo-Australian, Philippine, Caroline, Bismarck, Fiji, Scotia and Antarctic plates.
issues: The names are printed as "Mickenze and Parker"; the 1967 paper was by Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker. Also, "Tectonic" comes from the Greek for "building/construction", not "movement". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Outline drawing of the continents cut apart (Eurasia, Africa, India, Greenland, North America, Antarctica, South America, Australia).
Map captioned "Plate Tectonics in Pakistan": the Eurasian, Indian, Arabian and African plates with the plates boundary (red line) and northern Pakistan circled.
issues: The Chaman Fault runs along Pakistan's western (Balochistan–Afghanistan) side; the plate boundary in the north (where the 2005 earthquake struck) follows the Main Mantle/Himalayan thrust faults. Saying "Pakistan lies on Chaman Fault line" simplifies this. Recorded as printed.

issues: Igneous rocks form from both lava (at the surface — extrusive) and magma cooling underground (intrusive, e.g. granite and gabbro); the opening sentence mentions only lava. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Map captioned "World distribution of Volcanoes": the "Ring of Fire" shaded around the Pacific Ocean with major active volcanoes marked, and the Eurasian, North American, Philippine, Pacific, Cocos, Caribbean, Nazca, South American, Indian-Australian and Antarctic plates labelled.
issues: The MBT actually separates the Lesser Himalaya from the Sub-Himalaya (Siwaliks); the boundary between the Greater and Lesser Himalaya is the Main Central Thrust. "Main Boundary Fault" is another name for the MBT, so items i and iv describe the same structure. Recorded as printed.
Strictly, "hot spots" are volcanoes fed by mantle plumes inside plates (e.g. Hawaii); volcanoes at diverging boundaries (e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) are not hot spots as a rule. Recorded as printed.

The grid figure is a simplified redraw of the book's topographic sheet; exact positions of villages and contours are approximate. Readers should use the printed map for six-figure grid-reference practice.

The glossary says distribution maps show "aerial distribution"; the correct word is "areal" (by area). In a normal fault the movement is mainly vertical/down-dip along a sloping fault plane. Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Distance from the sea": continental areas (areas farther from sea) of North America, South America, Europe/Asia and Africa shaded, coastal areas marked, and the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Southern Oceans labelled.
Illustration captioned "Temperature and Altitude": a mountain with snow-capped peaks and a hot-air balloon, with temperature markers at sea level and at 1000 m steps.
World map captioned "Tropical Rain Forest" (titled "TROPICAL RAINFORESTS OF THE WORLD", scale 0–14,000 km) with the Amazon Basin, Congo Basin and South-East Asian islands shaded dark green.
issues: Tropical climates are usually defined as having every month's average at or above 18°C (a minimum), not an "average monthly temperature" of 18°C. Recorded as printed.
"lightening" should be "lightning". Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Hot Deserts": principal regions of hot deserts shaded red — south-western USA/Mexico, coastal Peru/Chile, the Sahara, Arabia, Iran–Thar, the Kalahari/Namib and central Australia — with the Gobi/Central Asian deserts shaded yellow.
issues: The Thar Desert lies in both Pakistan and India (mostly India); the Kalahari and Namib are in southern Africa (Botswana, Namibia), not the country "South Africa" alone. Recorded as printed.
The 57.8°C reading at Al-Azizia (1922) was officially invalidated by the World Meteorological Organization in 2012; the accepted world record is 56.7°C at Death Valley, USA. Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Savanna Climate" (scale 0–14,000 km): savanna areas shaded dark blue in South America, central and East Africa, India/South-East Asia and northern Australia.
issues: The temperature thresholds read awkwardly: middle-latitude (temperate) climates are usually defined by the coldest month averaging between about −3°C and 18°C and the warmest month above 10°C. Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Temperate (Steppes) Climate": the Prairies, Steppes (Eurasia), Pampas, Veld and Downs shaded green.
issues: Tasmania and New Zealand mostly have a marine west-coast (oceanic) climate rather than a true Mediterranean climate. Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Mediterranean Climatic Region": California, Central Chile, the Mediterranean Sea lands, the south-western tip of Africa and south and south-western Australia shaded green.
issues: The book's map latitude labels mark the Mediterranean region near 0°–30°N and California near the equator; the grid labels on the printed map are misplaced (the Mediterranean lies at about 30°–45°N). Recorded as printed.

decorative: World map captioned "Tundra": tundra regions shaded red across northern North America and its islands, the coastland of Greenland and northern Europe and Asia.

issues: Typical Mediterranean vegetation is evergreen broad-leaved shrubs and trees (olive, cork oak, maquis scrub); conifers grow mainly on its mountains. Recorded as printed.
Buffalo grass is actually a short grass of the dry western prairie, while bluestem is the typical tall grass. Recorded as printed.
